title: Roadway Design Compiler
pitch: Agent-native roadway design in the browser, powered by 39 WebMCP tools, a real geometry kernel, terrain-aware intelligence, and seamless vendor-neutral LandXML export.
about_excerpt: Agent-native roadway design in the browser, powered by 39 WebMCP tools, a real geometry kernel, terrain-aware intelligence, and seamless vendor-neutral LandXML export. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Roadway design has an unusually clear line of authority: a licensed Professional Engineer reviews, approves, and seals the work and carries personal legal responsibility for it. An agent can calculate geometry, generate alternatives, and prepare deliverables, but it cannot inherit that accountability. That made roadway engineering a strong test for WebMCP. The question was not simply “how much can the agent do?” It was: how can a website let an agent do real engineering work right up to, but never past, the point where a qualified human must decide? What it does Roadway Design Compiler is an agent-native conceptual roadway design studio with 39 WebMCP tools . From a supported agent, a user can ask the site to: read an existing design, alignment limits, curve and profile tables, cross sections, superelevation, terrain, and roadside quantities; author horizontal geometry, vertical profiles, cross-section templates, materials, template drops, coordinate systems, superelevation, and roadside items; import LandXML alignments, surfaces, site features, and as-designed reference sections; check configurable design criteria and propose multiple alternatives; create portable share links and prepare LandXML or construction-staking CSV deliverables. The key is the safety boundary. Every agent-applied change is stamped agent-proposed and enters a visible change ledger. While any proposal is unconfirmed, the site refuses both LandXML and staking exports. There is deliberately no WebMCP tool that can clear that gate. A person must review and confirm the change in the UI. This is conceptual design tooling, not construction software. The built-in criteria defaults are illustrative rather than an adopted agency standard, and every design still requires review and sealing by a licensed Professional Engineer. Why WebMCP is the right fit Traditional browser automation can manipulate fields, but it does not give an agent a trustworthy engineering contract. WebMCP lets the site expose typed, domain-specific actions and explicit refusal states. The agent chooses what to ask for; a deterministic engineering kernel decides what is geometrically and mathematically true; the human retains authority over adoption and export. That division creates a better experience for both sides: The agent can inspect the complete design instead of guessing from pixels or scraping a complex interface. It can preview a change, explain consequences, and request a commit through a typed tool. The user sees the exact proposal and its provenance in the same UI used for manual design. Safety does not depend on a prompt. The site itself enforces the confirmation and export rules. People and agents can now collaborate on a complete roadway concept—geometry, profile, corridor, criteria, terrain, alternatives, and interoperable deliverables—without pretending that the agent can take the engineer's legal role. How we built it Prior work and hackathon additions Roadway Design Compiler is an existing project that we meaningfully extended with WebMCP during the submission period (August 25–September 3, 2026). Before this period, it included a deterministic roadway geometry kernel, the RoadDesign schema and validation, a form-based Studio, LandXML export, and initial RoadBench benchmark tests. It had no agent interface. During the submission period, we built all 39 WebMCP tools and their registration bridge, preview-and-commit workflows, structured refusals, the agent activity log, and the agent-proposed change ledger with its human confirmation gate. We also added design alternatives, undo for unconfirmed changes, portable design documents, LandXML import, terrain and reference-section visualization, pavement and roadside authoring, coordinate-system support, and construction-staking CSV export. Only work added during the submission period is offered for evaluation. Our repository's prior-work breakdown and dated commit history document the distinction between the existing foundation and the hackathon additions. The application is TypeScript end to end. It registers 39 tools through document.modelContext.registerTool and validates their inputs and the cross-field design document with Zod. Tool execution returns typed results and typed refusals, while an agent activity log records calls from inside the WebMCP execute path so judges can distinguish real tool use from DOM automation. The authoritative geometry layer is a pure deterministic kernel for horizontal alignment, vertical curves, corridor sections, design criteria, superelevation, and terrain sampling. No model sits in that path. A Three.js view renders the authored corridor and imported ground; plan, profile, curve, and section views provide inspectable engineering outputs. The LandXML 1.1/1.2 importer handles alignments, TIN surfaces, site features, and reference sections. It computes geometry from coordinates instead of trusting inconsistent direction metadata, refuses unsupported spirals rather than approximating them, and pre-scans very large files before building a DOM. Before the hackathon, the exporter had been round-tripped into Bentley OpenRoads Designer as a native alignment and profile; Bentley's own annotation reproduced the curve table to 0.01 ft. The app runs on Vite and is deployed on Cloudflare. The repository includes 525 automated tests plus driver-owned browser harnesses for WebMCP registration, preview isolation, refusal→solve→commit workflows, superelevation, sealing gates, import, terrain, persistence, share links, and live deployment verification. Challenges we faced Drawing a boundary that code can actually enforce A warning in a system prompt was not enough. The difficult part was making preview, commit, provenance, confirmation, undo, and export operate as one coherent transaction model. The safest capability is sometimes an intentional omission: there is no agent tool for human confirmation. Handling real-world LandXML without fabricating data Public LandXML files vary widely. Some direction values are radians, others are degrees, and many do not say which. Some files contain hundreds of thousands of surface elements but no usable alignment. Spirals appear frequently, but this kernel does not model them yet. We chose explicit refusals over silent approximation, because a wrong road that looks plausible is more dangerous than a clear error. Keeping engineering truth deterministic The agent should decide what question to ask, not what the answer should be. Geometry, stopping-sight-distance relationships, K values, superelevation, runoff, cut/fill sign conventions, and export contents are computed by tested code with every coefficient disclosed as an input. video_transcript_excerpt: This is roadway design compiler. I asked the agent to make a complete circle. It calls web MCP and the application rebuilds the road. Roadway design compiler is a browser roadway design environment with 39 tools exposed through web MCP. An agent can read the live model, propose changes, and apply them through the page. The road is now fitted to the surveyed ground. The height profile changes while the plan remains a closed loop. Watch the activity log. Every row is a real web MCP call, read, check, or apply. The application, not the model, runs the roadway calculations. Green applied entries show the browser accepting those changes. Here is the finished road in 3D with its fitted profile and adjusted banking. It still needs professional engineering review. Next, I ask for three closed loop alternatives and require a human choice before anything changes. The page returns three computed concepts. I select the oval and it becomes the active design. Now the agent fits that oval to the surveyed ground. Watch the flat height profile become a terrain following curve. The same route is now visible in three dimensions with its fitted roadway section. Next, I ask for a four-lane road at 150 mph. 14 checks fail, so the agent refuses to force it onto the survey. Asked again, the agent reads the terrain extent and proposes larger side alternatives. The chosen concept passes its illustrative radius check, but it is far larger than the available ground. In 3D, the road visibly runs far beyond the small terrain patch. Then I change my mind. One request restores the saved terrain fitted oval. The activity log confirms the document load, validation, and terrain checks.

live_observation.first_impression: A functional roadway design studio with alignment, vertical profile, cross-section, superelevation, computed geometry, and export controls.
live_observation.action_attempted: Clicked Example to exercise the design input workflow.
live_observation.after_state: The studio displayed populated geometry and computed curve/vertical-curve tables, with LandXML and staking CSV download controls.
live_observation.notes: The page exposes a substantial engineering workflow rather than a static marketing screen.
